River flooding from upstream excessive rain impacted the region, bringing the Missouri River to moderate flood stage. The Missouri River crested at 37.55 feet at the Decatur gauge at 03:45 CDT on 6/26. Flood stage at this gauge is 35.0 feet.

Excessive rainfall across much of eastern South Dakota resulted in river flooding along the Missouri River at the end of June. Moderate flood stage was observed along the Missouri, with the Blair river gauge cresting at 32.3 feet at 14:30 CDT on 6/27. Flood stage for this river gauge is 26.5 feet.

Excessive rainfall across much of eastern South Dakota resulted in river flooding along the Missouri River at the end of June. Excessive rainfall across much of eastern South Dakota resulted in river flooding along the Missouri River at the end of June. Moderate flood stage was observed along the Missouri, with the river gauge in Bellevue cresting at 33.84 feet on 6/29. Flood stage at this river gauge is 30.0 feet.

Excessive rainfall across much of eastern South Dakota resulted in river flooding along the Missouri River at the end of June. Moderate flood stage was observed along the Missouri, with the river gauge in Plattsmouth cresting at 31.75 feet on 6/29. Flood stage for this river gauge is 26.0 feet. At 8:26 pm on the 23rd, emergency management reported the first instances of flooding showing several photos of lowland flooding in multiple spots along the river east of Plattsmouth. At 12:32 pm CDT on 6/25, Cass County emergency management sent photos of flooding at the Plattsmouth boat dock. Lowland flooding persisted into 6/26, with emergency management sending the office pictures of flooded fields from Sullivan Drive and Lake Waconda. At 5:56 PM on the 27th, emergency management reported flooding at the Plattsmouth sewer lift station on the south side of Main Street.

Excessive rainfall across much of eastern South Dakota resulted in river flooding along the Missouri River at the end of June. Moderate flood stage was observed along the Missouri, with the river gauge in Nebraska City cresting at 24.35 feet on 6/30. Flood stage at this river gauge is 18.0 feet. At 10:20 am CDT, emergency management sent photos of minor flooding in industrial areas right along the riverbank. River flooding from upstream excessive rain impacted the region, bringing the Missouri River to moderate flood stage. The Missouri River crested at 37.55 feet at the Decatur gauge at 03:45 CDT on 6/26. Flood stage at this gauge is 35.0 feet. Additional flooding for the same reason was observed on Little Sioux River between 6/24 and 6/28. The Little Sioux river crested at 27.33 feet. Flood stage for this river in Monona County is 25.0 feet. At 04:56 am CDT on the 25th, law enforcement reported that a levee on the Little Sioux River failed 600 yards south of Highway 141 resulting in flash flooding in the surrounding areas. Later that same day shortly after 04:00 pm CDT, law enforcement reported a second levee breach near Rodney. By this point, water had breached the levee system on both sides of the river, resulting in several road closures and evacuations of nearby homesteads. Damage to this county from the flood was estimated to be $1,298,600.00.

Excessive rainfall across much of eastern South Dakota resulted in river flooding along the Missouri River at the end of June. Moderate flood stage was observed along the Missouri, with two Omaha river gauges cresting between 32.5 and 33.0 feet. Flood stage for this stretch of the Missouri ranges from 27.0 to 27.5 feet. At 3 pm, emergency management closed down Gifford Road in Council Bluffs as flood waters had reached the edge of the travel portion of the roadway. At 5:52 pm CDT on 6/25, Iowa Department of Transportation closed the I-680 Exit 1 westbound off-ramp as it became impassible due to flooding. By noon on 6/26, water was observed flowing over portions of the interstate and over lowlands into nearby farm fields. Later into the evening of the 26th, Iowa Department of Transportation reported numerous agricultural and local levee breaches west of Interstate 29 and north of Interstate 680 resulting in the rapid submerging of roads in this area. By 10:00 pm CDT, emergency management reported water to the shoulder of Interstate 29. By the morning of the 27th, water was observed on traffic cameras as covering segments of Interstate 29, primarily around mile marker 67.2 and north of Honey Creek. At 7:47 am CDT on the 29th, emergency management sent drone photos of I-29 completely submerged at and north of the I-680 interchange. Multiple ramps at the interchange were also submerged. At 3:30 pm CDT on the 29th, emergency management reported the waters had begun to recede, partially uncovering previously flooded stretches of Interstate 29. Damage in this county from the flood was estimated to be $637,250.00.

This tornado developed immediately prior to the dissipation of the Lincoln EF-3 tornado to its southeast. The tornado traveled northeast for nearly 3 miles, doing most of its damage to trees and powerlines, but also destroying two large outbuildings and causing window damage to a home. Peak estimated winds in this tornado were at 107 miles per hour, with a peak width of 150 yards and an average track width estimated at 100 yards.

A narrow area, less than 100 yards across with several damaged trees and downed limbs was documented along Highway 15. Roads off of the highway near this location were impassable. This damage lines up perfectly with tight radar indicated rotation, and with a funnel observation. Peak winds in this tornado were estimated at 74 miles per hour. The width of this tornado was measured to be at 80 yards.

This tornado touched down along SW 27th street just south of West Rokeby Road and quickly produced EF1 damage as it moved northeast. Extensive tree damage was noted to several acreages along the path to the south of Rokeby Road. A horse boarding facility sustained significant damage where 6 small stable barns were destroyed. The tornado crossed north of Rokeby Road shortly after hitting the horse farm, moving more east, nearly parallel to Rokeby Road for about a mile. During this time, a few acreages sustained significant damage. Half of an outbuilding was completely destroyed as well as a large silo. The tornado continued east of SW 12th Street damaging large trees before lifting just east of South 1st street.

A line of intense thunderstorms swept across Sarpy county, resulting in widespread significant wind damage. While the greatest measured wind gust was 80 miles per hour, recorded by a mesonet station in Papillion, narrow swaths of enhanced straight line wind damage was consistent with wind speeds closer to 100 miles per hour. One such swath impacted portions of northeast Gretna, where multiple homes had windows blown out, trees uprooted, and large portions of their roofs blown off. Most of this damage was noted around the intersection of 168th Street and Meridian Street. Additionally, numerous powerlines and traffic lights were damaged or blown down across the county. Multiple semis were also noted as being flipped off of the road, one in north Gretna off of 204th street, and another off of Highway 370 in east Gretna. Power outages lasted for several days after the storms moved through. Total damages from these storms were estimated to be around 15 million dollars, with approximately 10 million in damages to the OPPD infrastructure.

A line of intense thunderstorms swept across the entirety of Douglas County, impacting the largest metropolitan area in the Omaha  NWS County Warning Area. As these storms entered the western part of the county, 80 miles per hour wind gusts were likely being produced, with a 76 miles per hour wind gust measured at the Omaha National Weather Service, and a 75 miles per hour wind gust measured by a mesonet station in west Millard. As the storms moved east across the county, the winds continued to intensify with widespread significant damage to trees, powerlines, and structures. In Waterloo, a roof was blown off of a commercial building, and in Midtown, a storefront awning and front fa��ade was completely destroyed. Wind gusts in the area were measured as high as 90 miles per hour, both by the Eppley Airfield ASOS and a mesonet station in Bennington. As such, straight line winds were estimated to be as high as 100 miles per hour with these storms as they moved through the Omaha metro. Power outages lasted for a week in some areas of the county, with OPPD estimated approximately 20 million dollars in damage in the county. Total damages from these storms are estimated to be 35 million in Douglas county alone.

A supercell thunderstorm caused cyclic tornadic activity southwest of Johnson.  As one tornado to the west was dissipating this one formed.  Eyewitnesses stated they saw both tornadoes on the ground at the same time for a while.  This tornado caused damage to several farmsteads southwest of Johnson.  A barn was blown down at one farmstead and other farm outbuildings and trees sustained major damage along its track.  Two houses also had some roof damage.  This supercell thunderstorm then spun up a third tornado a mile southwest of Johnson after this tornado had lifted or dissipated.

A supercell thunderstorm caused cyclic tornadic activity southwest of Johnson.  This tornado caused tree and farm outbuilding damage along its path.  As this tornado was dissipating, another one formed to the east.  Eyewitnesses stated they saw both tornadoes on the ground at the same time for a while.  The supercell thunderstorm then spun up a third tornado a mile southwest of Johnson.

A brief tornado caused scattered tree and farm outbuilding damage southeast of Falls City.  Another tornado, stronger and longer lived, formed several miles to the north of this one from the same supercell thunderstorm.

Heavy rain over sections of the Missouri River basin on June 4th and 5th, that eventually brought significant flooding downstream of Sarpy county, caused high water and some flooding along sections of the river in Sarpy county.  A camp ground and marina near the river in the southeast part of town was flooded for a while on Thursday June 5th into Friday the 6th.

Rainfall of 2 to 3 inches fell in a 2 to 3 hour period across sections of Saunders county.  The heavy rain produced flash flooding across Highway 92 east of Mead and also flooded farmland in the area.

Rainfall of around 3 inches in an hour and a half fell across sections of western Sarpy county. The heavy rain produced flash flooding of a couple of subdivisions in the Gretna area with 6 basements flooded.  The flood waters came from a cornfield to the west with debris from the field crossing a road in the subdivision.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 70 mph downed several large trees and some power lines at a Salvation Army Camp south of Offutt AFB.
Three inches of rain in around 1 hour caused flash flooding across a few streets in the Hamburg area.  The Willow Slough area near Argyle Street was especially affected.
A high-based narrow funnel cloud was caught and film south of Avoca.  The funnel apparently did not touch down, and if it did no damage was reported.

A swath of destructive straight line winds impacted portions of southeast Richardson County including Falls City. The Falls City ASOS measured a 91 miles per hour wind gust at 1:09 pm CDT, and again at 1:12 pm CDT. The ASOS lost power and stopped transmitting data at 1:15 pm CDT. Widespread tree damage was reported across Falls City with snow plows assisting in the removal of tree debris. Trees went through the roofs of two homes, and an additional house had a wall blown down as reported by law enforcement. A large factory in town lost approximately 3 to 4 thousand square feet of its roof. Powerlines were down across the southeast portion of the county, debris was strewn out across fields, and a school bus was reported to have been moved by the wind.

At approximately 5:55 PM CST on Thursday, April 17, a tornado developed near Highway 133, and appeared to produce first damage by snapping limbs in an area of trees. The tornado moved to the east, impacting trees, homes, and destroying a garage near 108th Street. It damaged trees along Little Papillion Creek and then impacted a home and large garage near 84th Street, south of Dutch Hall Road. This was the point along the tornado track where the most intense damage was observed, as a well-built all-brick home was destroyed with only some walls still standing. Tree damage near the site, as well as the destruction of a large, well-built garage, supported the estimate of high-end EF-2 to low-end EF-3 damage at this location. The tornado proceeded to destroy another large shed, and remove the roof from a brick home a half mile to the east. It then destroyed a very large garage-type building in-between two homes at 78th Street south of Dutch Hall Road. The tornado passed directly between the homes, causing extensive tree damage, lifting and moving a full-size pickup truck approximately 30 yards, and throwing large trees nearly a quarter of a mile downstream. The tornado weakened slightly but damaged several outbuildings and trees near 72nd Street. The peak width of the tornado during this segment of its track was measured at 170 yards with a length of 3.88 miles. The maximum wind speed during this segment of its track was estimated at 140 mph, 0 fatalities and 0 injuries.

This is a continuation of the Douglas County segment of this EF-3 tornado. At the start of this segment, the tornado began to move more northeasterly, snapping several trees and flipping recreational vehicles at Nashville, NE. It directly impacted another home, destroying two outbuildings and causing tree damage near Country Road P38, supporting the estimate of EF-2 damage. The tornado impacted one more home and destroyed another outbuilding near Country Road P51 before dissipating in an open field at approximately 6:15 PM CST. The peak width of the tornado during this segment of its track was measured at 170 yards with a length of 4.24 miles. The maximum wind speed during this segment of its track was estimated at 120 mph, 0 fatalities and 0 injuries.

At approximately 6:14 PM CST on Thursday April 17, video evidence supports the development of a tornado near 250th St and Alvo Road. Little to no damage was reported, even to trees, as it passed through multiple wooded areas. The tornado appeared to have a maximum width of less than 50 yards with a length of 0.84 miles. The maximum wind speed during this segment of its track was estimated at 60 mph, 0 fatalities and 0 injuries.

At approximately 6:20 PM CST on Thursday, April 17, video evidence supports the development of a tornado near 286th St and McKelvie Road that lasted for approximately 2 minutes. No damage was reported as it passed through open fields, supporting an EF-U rating.

At approximately 6:36 PM CST on Thursday April 17, a intermittent tornado developed southwest of Manley, NE based on video evidence. Intermittent tornado circulation passed through mainly open fields, but also through some areas of trees with little to no damage, supporting an EF-1 rating. The maximum wind speed during this track was estimated at 50 mph, 0 fatalities and 0 injuries.

Approximately 7:13 PM CST on Thursday, April 17, 2025, a tornado formed 3 miles southwest of Tabor, IA. The tornado stirred up copious amounts of dust and dirt from recently plowed agricultural field. The tornado moved southeast across mainly agricultural fields until cross U.S. 275, producing EF-0 damage to roofs and farm outbuildings just south of 130th Street, reaching a width of about 1/4 mile. Based on video, the tornado weakened briefly east of U.S. 275 until it crossed 280th Avenue, where it again reached a width of about 1/4 mile and strengthened again before crossing 290th Avenue, producing EF-0 damage to trees and flipping irrigation pivots. The tornado continued until about the intersection of 300th Avenue and 140th Street where it dissipated at approximately 7:28 PM CST. The maximum wind speed during this track was estimated at 85 mph, 0 fatalities and 0 injuries.

At approximately 7:32 PM CST on Thursday, April 17, a tornado formed southeast of Randolph, IA. The first sign of damage was snapped tree limbs near Lake Shawtee. As the tornado progressed eastward, continued tree damage was observed along with the damage of small outdoor farm buildings and house roofs. A concentrated area of the most extensive damage was observed south of Imogene, IA. In this area, damage included snapped wooden power poles, minor damage to homes, and the continued damage of outdoor buildings and trees. The width of damage also reached its peak, approximately 1971.2 yards in this area. The maximum wind speed during this segment of the track was estimated at 110 mph, classifying it as an EF1, 0 fatalities and 0 injuries.

This is a continuation of the Fremont County segment of this EF-1 tornado. The tornado tracked just north of Essex, IA, with more wooden power poles snapped and farm outdoor building damage. After sliding north of Essex, IA, the tornado tracked northeast towards Nyman, IA. Similar damage, including trees, outdoor buildings, and wooden power poles were observed along this stretch. The tornado lifted just east at Nyman, IA at approximately 8:08 PM CST. The maximum wind speed during this segment of the track was estimated at 110 mph, classifying it as an EF1. The tornado had a maximum width of 1219 yards, 0 fatalities and 0 injuries.

During the late afternoon hours of April 24, 2025, a supercell tracked over the Omaha metropolitan area, with rainfall totals of 2.5 to 3.5 inches along a swath from Ralston in SW Omaha through northwestern Pottawattamie County led to flash flooding in portions of Omaha. Considerable flooding was reported in the Saddle Creek area with water up to the windows of vehicles and dumpsters floating.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across Antelope county in April. The cooperative observers at Elgin, Oakdale, and Royal 2SE recorded 0.81, 0.75, and 0.65 inches of precipitation for the month, respectively.  These values were 1.98 to 2.77 inches below average.

The cooperative observers at Albion and Loretto 7W recorded 0.91 and 0.81 inches of precipitation for the month, respectively. These values were 1.76 and 1.81 inches below average.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across nearly the western half of Pierce county in April. The cooperative observer at Pierce recorded 1.85 inches of precipitation for the month. This was 0.99 inches below average.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across roughly the western two thirds of Madison county in April. The Norfolk Airport ASOS recorded 1.22 inches of precipitation for the month. This was 1.51 inches below average.

Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across the northwestern corner of Platte county in April. The cooperative observer at Columbus 3NE recorded 1.82 inches of precipitation for the month. This was 1.11 inches below average.

A tornado developed on the Platte River just west of County Road 3 at 4:29 PM CST. The tornado moved east on the river before coming on the north shore where it damaged some campers and mobile homes, as well as cottonwood and maple trees. This included one very large cottonwood tree which was uprooted and fell on to a home. The life cycle of the tornado was evaluated using time stamped video from storm chasers. The final part of the track was intermittent, and the entire tornado lasted for approximately 2 minutes and 30 seconds. Damage to trees and homes indicated a narrow swath of peak estimated wind speed of 90 to 100 mph.

D2 (severe) drought continued across the southwest portion of the county through May, with a narrow sliver of D3 (extreme) drought conditions along the southwestern county border. The cooperative observers at Crofton, Orchard 9NNE and Verdel 6SSE recorded 4.01, 5.24, and 4.65 inches of precipitation for the month, respectively. These values were 0.16, 1.44, and 0.85 inches above average.

D3 (extreme) drought conditions were introduced to a majority of the county at the beginning of the month and continued through the remainder of the month. The cooperative observer at Oakdale recorded 2.43 inches of precipitation for the month. This value was 1.59 inches below average.

D2 (severe) drought conditions persisted across the majority of the state with a narrow region of D3 (extreme) drought in the northern portion of the county. The cooperative observers at Albion and Loretto recorded 3.60 and 3.47 inches of precipitation for the month, respectively. These values were 0.51 and 0.77 inches below average.

At the beginning of the month, D3 (extreme) drought conditions were introduced across the extreme western portion of the county with a D2 (severe) drought in place across the western half of the county. Through the month, the area of D2 drought expanded to nearly the rest of the county. The cooperative observer at Pierce recorded 2.0 inches of precipitation for the month. This value was 1.78 inches below average.

At the beginning of the month, D3 (extreme) drought conditions were introduced across the extreme western portion of the county with a D2 (severe) drought in place across the western half of the county. The Norfolk Airport ASOS recorded 1.98 inches of precipitation for the month. This value was 1.91 inches below average.

D2 (severe) drought conditions persisted across the western half of the county through the month. The cooperative observer at Columbus 3 NE recorded 4.51 inches of precipitation for the month. This value was 0.06 inches above average.

Toward the middle of the month, a D2 (severe) drought was introduced across the western portion of the county. Through the remainder of the month, conditions improved enough to trim back the D2 drought to the southwest corner of the county. The cooperative observer at Surprise recorded 3.74 inches of precipitation for the month. This value was 1.00 inches below average.

Toward the middle of the month, a D2 (severe) drought was introduced across the majority of Seward county.  Through the remainder of the month, conditions improved enough to trim back the D2 drought to the northwest corner of the county. The cooperative observer at Seward recorded 3.37 inches of precipitation for the month. This value was 1.37 inches below average.

Toward the middle of the month, a D2 (severe) drought was introduced into a majority of Lancaster county. Through the remainder of the month, conditions improved enough to remove the D2 drought from the county. The cooperative observer at Crete 4ESE recorded 2.88 inches of precipitation for the month. This value was 2.61 inches below average.

On the morning of August 9, 2025, flash flooding struck the Blair, Nebraska area, particularly Southern Washington County, following a storm that delivered 3 to 4 inches of rain. Rainfall rates peaked at 2.5 to 3 inches per hour. Public reports confirmed significant impacts, including 6 to 10 inches of fast-moving water flowing through an apartment complex parking lot, and striking photos of residential backyards inundated with 3 to 5 feet of standing water. Minor flooding was also observed along Cauble Creek.

On the morning of August 10, 2025, heavy thunderstorms pushed through the Lincoln, Nebraska metropolitan area, triggering flash flooding across northwest Lincoln and north-central Lancaster County. Measured rainfall totaled 3.12 to 3.69 inches, with radar estimates confirming a similar 3 to 4-inch range. The intensity of the storm was the primary factor, with rainfall rates peaking at a severe 1.5 to 2.5 inches per hour. Public reports included major travel disruption, with Cornhusker Highway completely covered in water between Interstate 180 and Highway 77 at 1:55 AM CST.

Heavy thunderstorms generated flash flooding across Mills County, Iowa, particularly in the western portion, on the morning of August 10, 2025. Rainfall totals were measured between 3.1 and 3.96 inches, though radar estimates indicated up to 3 to 5 inches across the area. The deluge was extremely rapid, with rainfall rates peaking at a dangerous 2 to 3.5 inches per hour. The resultant flash flood caused severe ground instability, with Emergency Management reporting multiple road washouts and mudslides in the environmentally sensitive Loess Hills region.

A strong line of severe thunderstorms swept across Saline County, Nebraska, on the morning of August 9th, 2025, producing a swath of damaging straight-line winds, particularly impactful across the northern portion of the county. The damage swath extended from the area around Friend eastward toward Dorchester and then southeast to Crete.||The most intense winds were reported in Friend, where an emergency manager documented widespread damage including trees down, power outages, roof damage to businesses, and estimated winds gusting between 80 to 90 mph. A separate measured report from an emergency manager in Friend measured a wind gust of 84 mph. Further impressive damage was reported east of Friend, near Dorchester, where emergency management noted wooden power poles snapped for approximately 10 miles, with winds estimated at 90 mph in this area.||Moving southeast, the damaging winds continued to affect the Crete area, where a measured gust of 64 mph was recorded by a public weather station 6 miles south-southwest of Friend. Other public reports from Crete included a large tree down around the intersection of 8th or 9th Street and Grove Avenue, as well as large tree branches falling onto a house. Winds in the Crete area were estimated to be between 70 to 80 mph. A less damaging, measured gust of 58 mph was also reported south-southeast of Dorchester.||The collective property damage to public infrastructure from this damaging wind swath is estimated to be $16,129,296.00. This figure reflects only the costs associated with repairing public assets and does not account for the extensive damage sustained by private and commercial properties throughout Saline County.

A damaging wind event tracked across Seward County, Nebraska, on the morning of August 9th, 2025, impacting areas from the southwest to the eastern portion of the county. The storm produced a number of strong, measured wind gusts, with the highest recorded being 82 miles per hour from a public weather station 3 miles south-southwest of Seward. Other measured gusts were consistently severe, including 80 miles per hour 2 miles south of Milford, and 76 miles per hour 2 miles southeast of Seward, indicating a widespread high-wind event across the county.||The measured gusts translated into significant damage, with numerous reports estimating winds in the 70 to 80 miles per hour range. Structural damage was reported by an NWS employee 4 miles south-southwest of Garland, where a roof was torn off a shed and large trees were downed. Elsewhere, public reports detailed large trees down on a house and vehicle 3 miles east of Cordova, and a large tree impacting a roof in Seward. These widespread tree and minor structural damage incidents contributed to a final damage cost estimate for public infrastructure of $1,411,213.00. This estimate covers only public assets and infrastructure and does not reflect the total damage sustained by private homes and businesses.

A severe thunderstorm moved through the northwest portion of Lancaster County, Nebraska, generating a swath of very strong winds on the morning of August 9th, 2025. The most intense wind report was an estimated gust of 100 mph from an emergency manager in Malcolm at 03:58 CST, which was associated with significant damage in the area, including snapped telephone poles holding the football field lights.||Widespread damaging wind gusts were observed or measured by multiple public and Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) stations, with several reporting wind speeds exceeding 80 mph. These included an 82 mph measured gust at the Lincoln Airport ASOS station 5 miles west-northwest of Lincoln, an 81 mph measured gust near Valparaiso, and an 84 mph measured gust east-southeast of Raymond.||The damaging winds resulted in noteworthy property damage across the impact area. Near Malcolm, an overturned camper led to five injuries, with two people transported for treatment. Substantial structural damage was also reported, including a law enforcement report of substantial roof damage to two buildings south-southwest of Lincoln, with winds estimated in the 80-90 mph range. Large trees were downed in multiple locations, including one over a foot in diameter falling on a parked vehicle north-northwest of Lincoln. Numerous other trees were snapped off near the ground southwest of Lincoln and south of Malcolm.||The total damage to public infrastructure in Lancaster County from this severe wind event is estimated to be $3,409,322.00. This figure reflects only the costs associated with repairing public assets and does not account for the extensive damage sustained by private and commercial properties throughout Saline County.

A severe thunderstorm moved across the southeast portion of Saunders County, Nebraska, generating a swath of damaging straight-line winds on the morning of August 9th, 2025. Earlier in the event, winds estimated around 70-80 mph uprooted a large tree and caused shed roof damage in Memphis.||Additional, lesser wind gusts were measured by public weather stations across the area, ranging from 60 mph to 67 mph. The estimated property damage to public infrastructure from this event is $1,221,581.00. This figure reflects only the costs associated with repairing public assets and does not account for the extensive damage sustained by private and commercial properties throughout Saline County.

A highly damaging swath of severe thunderstorm winds moved across Douglas County, Nebraska, predominantly impacting the western and northern parts of the county, including the Omaha metropolitan area on the morning on August 9th, 2025. ||The storm produced damaging wind gusts, with the highest being an estimated 100 mph reported by broadcast media southwest of Washington at 04:52 CST. Multiple locations experienced estimated and measured gusts of 90 mph or higher. An estimated 95 mph gust was reported in Bennington, also responsible for destroying a shed. An estimated 95 mph gust and snapped power poles south of Valley. An estimated 95 mph gust and snapped trees with large diameters north-northeast of Elkhorn. Measured gusts by NWS employees up to 90 mph near Valley.||Tragically, significant impacts occurred east-southeast of Yutan at 04:55 CST when an estimated 90 mph gust uprooted a very large tree (approximately two feet in diameter) that fell onto a vehicle, resulting in one fatality and one injury. Widespread structural and tree damage impacted parts of the area. In Bennington, damage reports included the destruction of a shed and large snapped tree branches. Near Elkhorn, a large tree fell onto a truck and minivan. North-northeast of Valley, there was damage to a roof, resulting in insulation blown across the road, and an overturned semi-truck. The severe winds also downed power lines southwest of Washington and destroyed a boat canopy southeast of Washington.||The property damage to public infrastructure across Douglas County from these severe winds is estimated to be $3,810,332.00. This figure reflects only the costs associated with repairing public assets and does not account for the extensive damage sustained by private and commercial properties throughout Saline County.

A damaging wind event swept across Washington County, Nebraska, during the morning hours of August 9th, 2025, with a path of damage extending from the southwest to the eastern portion of the county. Measured wind reports indicated damaging wind speeds, with a maximum measured gust of 86 miles per hour reported by a public station 1 mile south-southeast of Blair. Widespread measured gusts throughout the county ranged from 58 miles per hour (recorded at the Blair Municipal AWOS) to 70 miles per hour.||However, the severity of the damage suggested straight-line winds were considerably higher, with the peak estimated wind speed reaching 110 miles per hour 1 mile south-southeast of Blair, where a building roof collapse was reported. Near Blair, the destruction was particularly acute; estimated 95 miles per hour gusts snapped large tree trunks, and estimated 90 miles per hour winds resulted in a very large tree fell onto a camper 4 miles northeast of Blair. Other reports of estimated 90 mph gusts included siding ripped off a garage and large trees (2-3 feet in diameter) downed near 2 SSE Kennard. Given the wide-scale damage to infrastructure, the estimated cost for public infrastructure repairs alone reached $2,699,403.00. This figure does not reflect the total economic damage, which includes the extensive losses sustained by private and commercial properties.

A damaging wind event tracked across Harrison County, Iowa, during the morning of August 9th, 2025. The storm swept across the county, producing a number of strong measured wind gusts, peaking at 76 miles per hour in Missouri Valley. Other significant measured gusts were 66 miles per hour, also in Missouri Valley, and 64 miles per hour 5 miles west-northwest of Persia.||The severity of the storm was highlighted by two reports of wind damage with significantly higher estimated wind speeds. The highest estimated wind gust of 100 miles per hour was reported in Pisgah, where public reports confirmed several trees down and a snapped power pole. An estimated 90 miles per hour gust was also reported in Mondamin, resulting in a large uprooted tree.

A severe wind event struck Jefferson County, Nebraska, during the morning of August 10th, 2025, impacting the area along a swath that extended from the southwest to the northeast portion of the county. The limited measured reports indicated gusts up to 65 miles per hour in Plymouth and 62 miles per hour 6 miles west-northwest of Fairbury. However, damage reports suggested pockets of much more intense winds occurred across the county.||The highest estimated wind speed was 95 miles per hour 4 miles west of Endicott, reported by Law Enforcement, which resulted in a power pole down and a corresponding power outage. Further east, an estimated 90 miles per hour gust caused significant damage to a large grain bin 2 miles west-southwest of Plymouth. Given these impacts to public utility and agricultural infrastructure, the damage cost estimated for public infrastructure was $29,813.00. This relatively lower figure indicates that while severe, the core damage was highly localized, and this estimate only covers damage to public assets, not private property losses.

A damaging wind event impacted Nemaha County, Nebraska, on the morning of August 10th, 2025, primarily affecting the northwest to north-central portion of the county. On the morning of September 1, 2025, thunderstorms brought heavy rainfall and subsequent flooding concerns to portions of eastern Nebraska, including southern Seward County. Radar estimates for the event indicated total rainfall amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches. These estimates were directly corroborated by public rainfall reports, which documented amounts such as 5.51 inches four miles northwest of Dorchester, NE, 4.43 inches five miles north of Dorchester, NE, and 3.97 inches three miles west-northwest of Milford, NE. By 6:35 AM CST, after the excessive rainfall had concluded, emergency management reported that the resulting runoff had caused water moving over numerous roads located south and west of Milford, NE.

On the morning of September 1, 2025, intense thunderstorms generated heavy rainfall and subsequent flooding concerns across portions of eastern Nebraska, specifically Seward County. Radar estimated total rainfall for the event ranged from 3 to 6 inches. These assessments were strongly supported by public rainfall reports, which documented significant totals, including 5.51 inches four miles northwest of Dorchester, NE, 4.43 inches five miles north of Dorchester, NE, and 3.97 inches three miles west-northwest of Milford, NE. The resultant runoff from this excessive precipitation led to riverine flooding in Seward County along the Big Blue River near Crete, NE. The river officially entered flood stage at 8:30 PM CST on September 1, 2025, and reached its maximum height, or crest, of 21.30 feet���a level corresponding to minor flood stage���at 12:30 AM CST on September 2, 2025. The Big Blue River subsequently receded and fell below flood stage at 4:30 AM CST on September 2, 2025.
Excessive rainfall across portions of eastern Nebraska led to river flooding along the North Oak Creek at Valparaiso. The river crested at 20.21 feet, minor flood stage.

Excessive rainfall across portions of eastern Nebraska triggered riverine flooding along the Wahoo Creek extending from September 1 into September 2, 2025. Initial impact was noted at 5:45 PM CST when a National Weather Service (NWS) employee reported water moving over Country Road J near Country Road 16. The river gauge at Wahoo Creek at Ithaca officially entered flood stage at 12:30 AM CST on September 2, 2025. The creek subsequently reached its crest of 19.55 feet, a level corresponding to minor flood stage, at 6:15 AM CST. By 9:00 AM CST on September 2, the gauge indicated that the Wahoo Creek had receded back below flood stage.

Rainfall of 2 to 3 inches fell over much of the Turkey Creek basin on October 21 and October 22.  The rain caused Turkey Creek to flood from near DeWitt to near and upstream of Wilber.  Turkey Creek near Wilber reached its first crest of around 12.7 feet during the late morning hours of October 23.  Due to heavy rains that fell on the 21st and 22nd across the upper reaches of the basin, the creek remained near that elevated level through mid afternoon on the 26th.  Flood stage is 11 feet.  Although a few county roads were flooded, the flooding mainly affected agricultural farmland.

Rainfall of 2 to 3 inches fell over much of the middle and upper sections of the Big Blue River basin on October 21 and October 22.  The rain caused the Big Blue River to flood for a prolonged period from Crete downstream to near DeWitt.  The river near Crete crested at 21.7 feet around 915pm CDT on 10/24, flood stage is 18 feet.  The flooding affected agricultural farmland and also closed a few county roads in the area.

Extreme (D3) drought conditions persisted across Antelope County through the month of April, though improvements in areal coverage were observed. The coverage of extreme drought shrank from nearly 97 percent at the beginning of the month down to around 65 percent by the end of the month. The cooperative observers at Elgin and Oakdale recorded 1.90 and 2.14 inches of precipitation, respectively. These values were 0.89 and 0.73 inches below average.

The cooperative observers at Albion and Loretto 7W recorded 2.46 and 2.38 inches of precipitation, respectively. These values were 0.21 and 0.24 inches below average.

A tornado developed approximately 1.5 miles north-northwest of Little Sioux, IA at 12:46 PM CST. The tornado began just southeast of the intersection of 120th Street and Dayton Avenue, before flipping a center pivot. It continued northeast, damaging farm outbuildings, trees, and power poles near 120th Street and Early Avenue. Just over 1 mile northeast of this intersection, another center pivot was flipped over. The tornado then turned slightly more eastward and tore the fabric roofing off part of a hoop barn near Gage Lane and Easton Trail. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 105 mph.

Several videos and photographs from multiple angles indicated that a weak tornado developed and moved to the east northeast along this approximate path. While the near-surface dust cloud was wider, the core circulation was quite narrow and weak. The only damage along the track was minor tree damage as it crossed mostly open fields. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 70 mph.

According to researchers tracking this storm, who were using DOW - a mobile radar system, this brief tornado touched down around 2 miles west southwest of exit 72 on Interstate 29 and lifted about 1/2 mile east of the exit.  The tornado downed 1 tree but did little other damage.  Besides being visually seen by the researchers, it also produced a tornadic signature on the DOW system.

This was the second tornado that was observed by researchers tracking this storm.  The tornado touched down briefly just northeast of exit 72 on Interstate 29 and lifted a little to the northeast, doing no apparent damage.  The researchers were using DOW, a mobile radar system, and besides being visually seen by the researches, it also produced a tornadic signature on the DOW system.

Rainfall of 2 to 3 inches fell across much of Saunders county on 10/21 and 10/22.  The heavy rain caused Sand Creek to flood around Wahoo and Wahoo Creek to flood from near Wahoo downstream through Ithaca to around Ashland.  Several county roads were flooded in this area as was Highway 92 west of Wahoo and Highway 77/92 near its Jct with Highway 109 east of town.  The flooding washed the gravel off of several county roads but otherwise damage was minimal and was restricted to river lowlands.

Rainfall of 2 to 3 inches fell over much of the middle and upper sections of the Big Blue River basin on October 21 and October 22.  The rain caused the Big Blue River to flood for a prolonged period from near Milford downstream to around DeWitt, which is in Saline County.  The river near Crete, which is in Saline county, crested at 21.7 feet around 915pm CDT on 10/24, flood stage is 18 feet.  The flooding affected agricultural farmland, closed a few county roads in the area and caused the delay of local bridge construction just south of Milford which was damaged by flooding over the summer.
Winds gusts estimated at close to 60 mph caused an old vacant building to collapse in Union.  The winds were the result of Canadian air spilling southeast across the plains.

Falling temperatures and strong northwest winds brought dangerously cold wind chill values to the area much of December 14th into the morning hours of the 15th.  Winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph and temperatures falling to the single digits above and then below zero produced wind chill values of 20 below to 30 below zero.  Wind chill values got even colder during the morning hours of the 15th as temperatures dropped even further.  The strong winds and cold temperatures were accompanied by snow showers and areas of blowing snow which reduced visibilities below a 1 mile occasionally during the afternoon of the 14th.  Snow accumulations were generally only a few inches.

An Arctic cold front that plunged southeast across the area brought falling temperatures and dangerously cold wind chill values.  As readings fell from the low single digits above zero during the morning of 12/20, to the low single digits below zero from the afternoon of the 20th through the afternoon of the 21st, wind chill values fell to 20 below to about 32 below zero. Northwest winds of 25 to 40 mph were reported during the morning through afternoon of 12/20 which caused significant blowing and drifting snow creating poor visibilities and closing many east-west roads.

New snowfall of an inch or two fell during the morning of 12/20.  This was on top of 5 to 10 inches that fell a few days prior.  As an Arctic front plunged across the area, northwest winds increased to 25 to 40 mph.  The strong winds caused significant blowing and drifting snow.  Visibilities frequently fell to a mile or less during this period and many east-west roads were blown shut.  In addition, falling temperatures and the strong winds created wind chill values of 20 below to 30 below zero.

Hail up to Softball size was reported in the Staplehurst area.
Hail between 1 inch and golf ball-size was reported from 1 mile south of Clatonia to 1 mile south of Cortland.
Hail up to 1 inch in diameter was reported just south and just east of Lincoln.  The hail fell from the supercell thunderstorm that produced several tornadoes southeast through east of town.

A supercell thunderstorm that produced several tornadoes southwest of town and at least one tornado northeast of town dropped hail across much of the Omaha metro area.  Across Omaha most of the hail was 1/2 inch in diameter or less, and it drifted several inches deep in some locations.  However, some larger hailstones were observed, mostly across the western sections of town.  Golf ball-size hail was reported near 144th and Ida, a few 1.25 inch stones fell near 150th and Blondo and 1 inch hail was observed near 168th and Harrison Streets.
Golf ball size hail was reported around 5 miles south of the southern part of Lincoln.
Reported near 132nd and Fort Streets.  From the second storm that rolled across the Omaha metro area this evening.

Emergency management spotted possibly two funnel clouds southeast of the the Jct of Highways 41 and 77 south of Cortland.  The funnels were from the same mini-supercell thunderstorm that produced a tornado north of Beatrice.
A tornado caused damage to a pole shed and roof of a house south of Pickerell.  Tree damage was also noted in this area.
Gradient east winds ahead of thunderstorms lifted and moved the roof of a quonset 25 yards.  The winds were estimated at over 60 mph.

Sustained winds of 35 to 40 mph with gusts of 60 to 65 mph prevailed over the county from late morning through early evening.  Several weather recording stations reported wind gusts of 60 to 65 mph including one maintained by emergency management which recorded a 65 mph wind gust at 258 pm CDT.  The strong winds downed trees and large limbs, power lines, caused some building damage in Fairbury and nearby Endicott and created very poor visibilities in blowing dust.  The winds also flipped 2 semis.  One semi was overturned southwest of Fairbury around 240 pm CDT and the other was blown over 1/2 mile east of Jansen on Highway 136 around 320 pm.  The second resulted in minor injuries to the driver.

Sustained winds of 35 to 40 mph with gusts of 60 to 65 mph prevailed over the county much of the afternoon of the 23rd.  A dept. of Roads sensor near Milford measured a 64 mph wind gust at 312 pm CDT.  The strong winds caused scattered tree, building and fence damage in the county.

Sustained winds of 35 to 40 mph with gusts of 50 to 55 mph prevailed over the county much of the afternoon of the 23rd.  One home weather station in Beatrice recorded sustained winds of 40 mph for several hours.

A dept. of roads sensor near Wilber measured sustained winds of 40 mph with gusts of 50 to 55 mph much of the afternoon of the 23rd.  The emergency manager in Wilber reported that a wind gust of 62 mph was measured by his home equipment.  The wind caused scattered tree and building damage in the county.  A semi trailer was also overturned near Dorchester.

The Asos at the Lincoln airport recorded sustained winds of 35 to 40 mph with gusts of 55 to 60 mph for several hours during the afternoon of the 23rd.  A peak gust of 60 mph was recorded at 248 pm CDT.
A thunderstorm wind gust was measured at 59 mph by Asos at the Falls City airport.  The winds caused damage to a hanger door.
A southerly thunderstorm wind gust was measured at 68 mph by the Asos at Omaha-Eppley airfield just behind a departing line of thunderstorms.
Hail 3/4 to 1.5 inches in diameter was reported from around Gretna northeast to the Chalco area.  There was also a rotating wall cloud reported in the Chalco area from this storm.
From the second severe storm to pass across the region this evening.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 60 mph damaged a metal outbuilding south of Claytonia.
Thunderstorm winds estimated at close to 60 mph blew the walls out of a machine shed.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 to 70 mph downed trees and snapped at least one power pole causing a power outage south of Salem.

Heavy snow and north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph brought blizzard conditions, especially in open areas, to Antelope county from the evening hours of April 4th until the morning of the 5th.  Although the snow decreased or ended by late morning on the 5th, the strong winds persisted through the afternoon causing continued drifting snow.  Snowfall of around 9 inches was reported in the Neligh area.  The snow and strong winds closed roads in the area.

Heavy snow and north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph brought blizzard conditions, especially in open areas, to Pierce county from the evening hours of April 4th until the morning of the 5th.  Although the snow decreased or ended by late morning on the 5th, the strong winds persisted through the afternoon causing continued drifting snow. Snow amounts were generally 4 to 6 inches across the county according to local newspaper reports.  Several roads were closed due to the snow and strong winds.

Heavy snow and north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph brought blizzard conditions, especially in open areas, to Boone county from the evening hours of April 4th until the morning of the 5th.  Although the snow decreased or ended by late morning on the 5th, the strong winds persisted through the afternoon causing continued drifting snow. Snow ranged from a trace to an inch or so in the southeast part of the county to 3 to 6 inches across the northwest section.  Snow amounts were estimated from reports in surrounding counties and visible satellite pictures depicting the snow cover the next day.

Heavy snow and north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph brought blizzard conditions, especially in open areas, to Knox county from the evening hours of April 4th until the morning of the 5th.  Although the snow decreased or ended by late morning on the 5th, the strong winds persisted through the afternoon causing continued drifting snow and whiteout conditions at times. Snowfall across the county was generally 4 to 7 inches with 7 inches in Bloomfield the heaviest reported.  The snow and wind closed roads in the area.

Heavy snow and north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph brought blizzard conditions, especially in open areas, to Cedar county from the evening hours of April 4th until the morning of the 5th.  Although the snow decreased or ended by late morning on the 5th, the strong winds persisted through the afternoon causing continued drifting snow. Snowfall over the county was generally between 4 and 7 inches, with 7 inches at Hartington the heaviest reported in Cedar county.  The snow and strong winds closed roads in the region.

Rain changed to a brief period of freezing rain then to a heavy wet snow during the late evening hours of April 4th and continued into the morning of the 5th.  The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the late morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours.  The ice and heavy wet snow caused scattered power outages across the county.  Snowfall amounts were reported to have been around 4 to 6 inches across the county based on newspaper reports, amounts received from surrounding counties and visible satellite imagery taken the next day.  Travel was extremely difficult at times.

Rain changed to a brief period of freezing rain then to a heavy wet snow around midnight CDT on April 5th and continued into the mid morning hours of that day. The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the late morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours.  The accumulated ice and heavy wet snow caused scattered power outages across the county and caused localized damage.  In Schuyler a grandstand roof was damaged and a section of a fence was blown down resulting in over $20,000 in damage. Snow amounts were between 4 and 8 inches across the county with 7 inches in Schuyler the heaviest reported.  Travel was extremely difficult at times.

Rain changed to a brief period of freezing rain then to a heavy wet snow around midnight CDT on April 5th and continued into the mid morning hours of that day. The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the late morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours.  Snowfall amounts were between 4 and 8 inches across the central and northern part of the county with an inch or so across the southeast.  Eight inches of snow was reported in Scribner and 7 inches at Uehling were among the heaviest. The ice and heavy wet snow and strong winds snapped power poles from around Scribner to Snyder and caused power outages in those areas north into Cuming county and southeast toward Hooper and also caused hazardous driving conditions. In some cases power was out until the evening of the 5th. Cell phone service was also interrupted due to a tower being blown down.

Rain changed to a heavy wet snow a little after midnight CDT on April 5th and continued into the mid morning hours of that day. The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the late morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours.  Snowfall amounts were between 6 and 10 inches across the county with 10 inches in Tekamah the highest reported.  The heavy wet snow caused over 2,000 customers to lose power due to downed power lines and poles.  Large tree limbs were also downed across the county.

This is the first of 5 cyclic tornadoes that a low-topped supercell thunderstorm produced at it tracked southeast through east of the Lincoln.  The first tornado touched down around 4 miles south of Hickman uprooting some trees and causing farm outbuilding and other tree damage along its path.

This is the second of 5 cyclic tornadoes that a low-topped supercell thunderstorm produced at it tracked southeast through east of the Lincoln area.  This tornado touched down around 2 miles east of Hickman and damaged a house in the area, destroyed some farm outbuildings, took the roof off of a barn and also caused tree damage.

This is the third of 5 cyclic tornadoes that a low-topped supercell thunderstorm produced at it tracked southeast through east of the Lincoln area.  This tornado touched down around 2.5 miles west of Bennet, in Lancaster county, tracked northeast clipping the far northwest corner of Otoe county and then lifted around 1.5 miles into the southwest corner of Cass county. In Lancaster county the tornado uprooted trees and caused farm outbuilding damage. In Cass county the tornado destroyed a garage and tossed the debris into a occupied car injuring 5 people.  The total path length was around 11 miles.

This is the third and longest tracked of 5 cyclic tornadoes that a low-topped supercell thunderstorm produced at it tracked southeast through east of the Lincoln.  This tornado touched down around 2.5 miles west of Bennet, in Lancaster county, tracked northeast clipping the far northwest corner of Otoe county and then lifted around 1.5 miles into the southwest corner of Cass county. In Otoe county the tornado caused tree and farm outbuilding damage.  In Cass county the tornado destroyed a garage and tossed the debris into a occupied car injuring 5 people.  The total path length was around 11 miles.

This is the third and longest tracked of 5 cyclic tornadoes that a low-topped supercell thunderstorm produced at it tracked southeast through east of the Lincoln area.  This tornado touched down around 2.5 miles west of Bennet, in Lancaster county, tracked northeast clipping the far northwest corner of Otoe county and then lifted around 1.5 miles into the southwest corner of Cass county. In Cass county the tornado destroyed a garage and tossed the debris into a occupied car injuring 5 people. Other tree and farm outbuilding damage was noted.  The total path length was around 11 miles.

This is the fourth of 5 cyclic tornadoes that a low-topped supercell thunderstorm produced at it tracked southeast through east of the Lincoln area.  This tornado touched down on the southwest side of Eagle and caused tree and some building damage along its path before lifting around 1 mile south of Alvo.  Three people sustained minor injures near Alvo when a tree fell onto a truck they were in.

This is the fifth and last of 5 cyclic tornadoes that a low-topped supercell thunderstorm produced at it tracked southeast through east of the Lincoln area.  This tornado touched down in Alvo and tracked a little over 10 miles north northeast before lifting just west of South Bend.  The tornado knocked down power poles and transmission lines, snapped trees and damaged houses and destroyed farm out buildings along its path.  One of the downed power lines fell on a car trapping its occupant for several hours.  Several cars were crushed by fallen trees in the Alvo area.  From the 3 confirmed tornadoes that hit the county, plus any associated wind damage, emergency management estimated that 30 homes had minor damage with 4 sustaining major damage and 60 to 80 farm outbuildings were damaged with the total damage approaching $1 million.

The tornado touched down near highway 30 about 1.5 miles west of the interchange between Interstate 29 and Highway 30, or about 3 miles west of Missouri Valley Iowa.  The tornado was at its strongest and widest within a mile of its touchdown point, becoming weaker with more intermittent damage farther north.  Near the touchdown point, a barn sustained roof damage and a windmill was knocked down.  One-half mile north of Highway 30, 54 empty grain rail cars were derailed.  One mile north of Highway 30, along 305th St., two residences were impacted by the tornado.  A 100-year-old single family residence directly in its path was completely destroyed, with all walls collapsed and debris relocated about 50 feet north of the foundation.  The debris collected over the site of a cinder block garage, which also partially collapsed.  About 100 yards north of the garage site, a machine shed was collapsed onto a combine inside, which had been moved by the wind.  Trees near the house sustained some broken limbs and treetops, and a power pole was snapped.  The damage at this site was given an EF2 rating.  Another residence one-quarter mile to its west sustained minor siding and shingle damage and windows were broken.  Seven of the eight outbuildings at that residence were collapsed, with debris strewn into nearby fields.  Damage at the two houses indicated a path width of one quarter mile at that point, the widest along the path of the tornado.  The tornado continued northward, overturning two semis on Interstate 29.  From there to a point about 3 miles southwest of Magnolia, near the intersection of the Loess Hills Trail and Melody Oaks Trail, intermittent light damage to trees and roofs of a couple of outbuildings was noted.  From this point, the survey team determined the damage path narrowed to 100 yards or less based on scattered tree and outbuilding damage, with EF0 intensity north of Interstate 29.

Scattered wind damage from a low-topped supercell thunderstorm that earlier produced 5 tornadoes to the south, was reported west through southwest of the South Bend area.  Due to the tree and farm outbuilding damage noted, a NWS Storm Survey estimated that wind speeds were between 90 and 100 mph.

Although snowfall from this storm across Antelope county was only an inch or two, it was accompanied by north winds of 30 to 35 mph with gusts of 50 to 55 mph.  This produced significant blowing and drifting snow closing several county roads and frequently reducing visibilities below 1/2 mile.

Snowfall of 1 to 3 inches was accompanied by north winds of 30 to 35 mph with gusts of 50 to 55 mph.  This produced significant blowing and drifting snow over the county closing many roads and frequently reducing visibilities below 1/2 mile.  Around 3 inches of snow from this storm was reported in Bloomfield for one of the higher amounts reported in the county.

Wind gusts estimated at close to 60 mph blew a storage shed located at the Tecumseh Livestock Auction into a power pole along Calhoun Street.  This caused power to be lost for around 45 minutes for about half the residents of Tecumseh, with a few customers without power for a day or two.  The winds were from gradient south winds that blew in advance of thunderstorms that developed west of region.  When the damage occurred, the line of thunderstorms was still about 20 to 30 miles to the west and moving north northeast.

Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 70 mph downed large trees and power lines around 9 miles southeast of Mondamin.  The winds were most likely rear flank downdraft winds that were wrapping around a tornado that was tracking near this location.

Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at around 70 mph caused damage to outbuildings, grain bins and trees around the Viking Lake area.  This damage could have either been associated with the tornado that a NWS storm survey determined to have touched down northeast of the lake, or from rear-flank downdraft winds from the storm.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 60 mph knocked a few large trees down across a road around 8 miles south of Stanton.

Gradient south winds of 35 to 40 mph with gusts to 50 to 55 mph prevailed for several hours across Boone county.  The winds severely damaged a barn 8 miles west of Albion and another one 11 miles west of town.

Freezing rain fell across the area for a while during the evening of March 9th followed by plunging temperatures and gusty North winds as an arctic air mass plunged into the region.  Although most ice accumulations were under 1/4 inch, the combination of ice and wind gusts of 40 mph or more caused scattered power outages from around Battle Creek to Elgin.  Ten sub-stations were knocked down due to the ice-wind combination causing 3500 customers to lose power.

Freezing rain fell across the area for a while during the evening of March 9th followed by plunging temperatures and gusty North winds as an arctic air mass plunged into the region.  Although most ice accumulations were under 1/4 inch, the combination of ice and wind gusts of 40 mph or more caused scattered power outages and closed a few schools and roads in the area.

Freezing rain fell across the area for a while during the evening of March 9th followed by plunging temperatures and gusty North winds as an arctic air mass plunged into the region.  Although most ice accumulations were under 1/4 inch, the combination of ice and wind gusts of 40 mph or more caused scattered power outages and closed a few schools and roads in the area.

Although most ice accumulations were under 1/4 inch, the combination of ice and wind gusts of 40 mph or more caused scattered power outages and closed a few schools and roads in the area.

Freezing rain fell across the area for a while during the evening of March 9th followed by plunging temperatures and gusty North winds as an arctic air mass plunged into the region.  Although most ice accumulations were under 1/4 inch, the freezing rain created very slick roads.  Ice-coated streets in West Point prevent firefighting equipment from making it up a hill to respond to a car fire in a duplex.  The firefighters had to park more than 100 yards away and drag the hose up a hill.  Several firefighters were injured when they slipped on the ice in the attempt.

Freezing rain fell across the area for a while during the evening of March 9th followed by plunging temperatures and gusty North winds as an arctic air mass plunged into the region.  Although most ice accumulations were under 1/4 inch, the combination of ice and wind gusts of 40 mph or more caused scattered power outages and closed a few schools and roads in the area.
Golf ball-size hail caused siding damage to at least 20 homes in the Dorchester area.

The tornado touched down near Tenville destroying trees at a cemetery, causing house and farm outbuilding damage in the area and other tree and roof damage along its path.  This tornado was from the same supercell that produced a tornado just to the south of here.

The tornado touched down just southwest of the intersection of 270th and Q Ave. west-southwest of Villisca.  Near that point the roof was torn off of an outbuilding and an empty grain bin was blown across the road.  A barn had some roof structure damage 2 to 3 miles north of there, near where the tornado apparently lifted.
A tornado apparently touched down on the Nebraska side of the Missouri River south of Springfield, SD.  The tornado caused some tree damage in the area.

Rain changed to a heavy wet snow a little after midnight CDT on April 5th and continued into the mid morning hours of that day. The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the late morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours.  The Cooperative observer near Little Sioux reported around 7.5 inches of snow from the storm ending around 7 am CDT.  Another inch or so fell during the morning, but much of that melted as it fell.

Rain changed to a heavy wet snow a little after midnight CDT on April 5th and continued into the mid morning hours of that day. The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the late morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours.  Public reports of snowfall included 8 inches in Pisgah and between 6 and 12 inches in the Moorhead area.  The heavy wet snow and strong winds caused scattered power outages in the county.

Wind gusts estimated at 60 to 65 mph tipped over 3 semi-trailer on Highway 2 from around 4 pm until 5 pm CDT.  The winds also destroyed a garage and snapped several pine trees near Palmyra around 630 pm.  The winds were from gradient south or southwest winds that blew in advance of and behind a line of thunderstorms that developed west of region and moved across the region.  The semis were tipped generally in advance of the storms, while the garage and tree damage occurred with the line 10 or 20 miles to the east.

Rain changed to a brief period of freezing rain then to heavy wet snow during the early morning hours of April 5th.  The snow continued into mid morning of that day.  The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours which caused difficult driving conditions due strong winds blowing across icy roads.  The ice, heavy wet snow and strong winds knocked down at least 75 power poles in the county which caused 3,000 customers to lose power.  The hardest hit area was north of David City.  Snowfall amounts were around 4 to 8 inches across the county, with 8 inches in David City the highest reported.

Rain changed briefly to a period of freezing rain then to a heavy wet snow in the late evening of April 4th with snow continuing into the mid morning hours of the 5th. The precipitation was accompanied by north winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 50 mph.  Although snowfall ended during the late morning of the 5th, the strong winds caused continued drifting snow in open areas into the afternoon hours.  Snowfall amounts were between 2 and 6 inches across the county based on reports from surrounding counties and satellite pictures taken the next day.  The ice and heavy wet snow and strong winds snapped power poles south of the county but some lines were downed causing power outages in the West Point, Wisner and Bancroft areas.  Travel was also very difficult.

Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked a few boards off of a farm outbuilding.  The winds were accompanied by pea-size hail.
A thunderstorm wind gust estimated at 60 mph was reported by a spotter near Treynor.
Hail up to ping pong ball size was reported in and around the Wisner area.
An occasional funnel that formed and dissipated several times was reported by a trained spotter near Coburg.
The public reported golf ball to baseball-size hail in Macedonia.  The reported was relayed to the NWS through a local TV station.
Hail the size of quarters was reported near 27th and Superior Streets in north Lincoln.
Hail up to nickel-size covered the ground east of Center.
Pea to quarter-size hail fell for around 10 minutes.
Penny to nickel-size hail fell along with very heavy rain.
Mostly pea-size but a few stones up to nickel-size.
One inch hail fell for several minutes in the Verdon area.
The hail was accompanied by thunderstorm wind gusts measured at almost 60 mph.
Hail 1 inch in diameter fell for several minutes in the De Witt area.  The hail was accompanied by 1.25 inches of rain in 40 minutes.
The cooperative observer near Plymouth measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 59 mph.  The winds were accompanied by hail up to 1 inch in diameter.

Heavy rain was reported across sections of Richardson county during the evening of June 1 with a little over 6 inches reported 6 miles south of Humboldt.  Law enforcement reported the rain caused minimal flooding or damage but 1 to 2 inches of water covered Highway 8 near mile marker 129, about 1/2 mile east of the Junction of Highways 105 and 8 for a while.

A prolonged period of hail entered Saline county near Tobias and proceeded through Swanton and De Witt where it caused considerable crop damage.  The hail covered the ground white and was a large as quarter-size in the Tobias area.

Quarter to half dollar-size hail was widespread from near Swanton to De Witt.  This hail storm caused significant crop damage in Saline county, especially across the southern part.  Emergency management estimated crop damages to corn, soybeans and winter wheat would run over a million dollars.  The damage was most significant along a 5 mile wide swath from around Tobias to Swanton to De Witt where the ground was covered white with hail.

Hail at least up to quarter-size fell across the northern part of Gage county near the Pickrell area.  The hail caused considerable crop damage in northern Gage county and was a continuation of the storm that caused over a million dollars of crop damage in Saline county.  In Gage county crop damage alone was estimated at $90,000.
Quarter-size hail covered the ground.
Quarter to half dollar-size hail was reported in the Cook area.
Golf ball-size hail was reported in Johnson by emergency management.
Home weather equipment of a trained weather spotter measured thunderstorm wind gusts at 58 mph.
Hail up to nickel size fell for at least 15 minutes in the area.
Hail up to half dollar-size was reported from 5 miles west of Fairbury to around 2 miles southwest of town.
Hail up to golf ball-size fell from around 4 miles south of Plymouth into Plymouth.
Quarter-size hail was reported from around 1 mile southwest of Western to around 1 mile east of town.
Quarter-size hail fell in the western and northwestern sections of Lincoln, from around the Cushman area through 27th and Superior Streets.

Reported from an off-duty NWS employee.
Hail up to quarter-size covered the ground from around the Norfolk airport through town.
Hail up to golf ball-size covered the ground from around 4 miles west of Rulo through Rulo and just northeast of town.

The hail lasted for around 5 minutes.
Hail up to half dollar-size was reported from the north part of Fairbury to 11 miles north of town.
Thunderstorm wind gusts measured by home weather equipment at 61 mph in the Plymouth area caused a tree to fall down onto a house.
Quarter-size hail was observed a little south of De Witt.  An unsubstantiated report of 2.5 inch hail was also received in the area.
The hail dented at least one car in the area.  The hail could have been larger according to the person who reported it the next day.

Hail up to half dollar-size was accompanied by thunderstorm winds that also downed a few trees.  The wind driven hail damaged numerous homes and cars in and around Adams and also caused crop damage in the area.  One local insurance agent had already received 50 agriculture/crop claims and 150 house and auto claims by Monday morning June 8th, with many, many, many claims against roof, siding and paint damage to come he stated.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 60 mph downed a few trees in the area.  The winds were accompanied by half dollar-size hail.
From the storm that also produced wind damage in the Plymouth area.
A thunderstorm downburst tore the roof off of a barn southeast of Auburn.  The winds were estimated at over 60 mph.
Heavy rain, for the second night in a row, caused flash flooding along Big Muddy Creek north of Falls City.  The flooding closed Highway 73 for an hour or so.  Damage along Highway 73 was minimal.
Nickel-size hail was reported along Interstate 80.
Hail up to half dollar-size fell for a little over 5 minutes near Tamora.

Heavy rain for the second night in a row caused flash flooding along Rock Creek and another unnamed creek near Salem.  The flooding crossed several county roads causing some gravel washout and culvert damage.
The first round of hail from a multi-updraft supercell thunderstorm that moved across the area this afternoon.  The hail caused some crop damage in the area.
The first round of hail from a multi-updraft supercell thunderstorm that moved across the area this afternoon.

Hail between 1 inch and 3 inches in diameter fell from around 5 miles southwest of Fairbury into Fairbury.  The hail fell from a multi-updraft supercell thunderstorm that moved across the area this afternoon and caused house and automobile damage.
From a multi-updraft supercell thunderstorm that moved across the area this afternoon.
A brief tornado touchdown was observed south of Odell and caused no apparent damage.  The tornado, or funnel before it touched down, had two vorticies for a while.

Hail up to baseball-size and even a few maybe up to softball-size fell from west of Odell across the south part of town and then to 2 miles south of town.  The hail caused house and automobile damage in and around town.  Some crop and tree damage was also reported.  The hail was driven by winds that were estimated to be at least 50 mph.

Hail up to golf ball-size was reported from southwest of Falls City into town.  Many vehicles in town sustained hail damage, some substantially, along with roofs and sidings of homes.  The hail was from a multi-updraft supercell thunderstorm that moved across the area that afternoon.
The ground was covered in hail up to golf ball-size.

Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 60 mph downed two trees onto a house along Highway 57.  The winds were accompanied by hail up to 2 inches in diameter.
The hail was accompanied by thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 mph and 1 inch of rain in 15 minutes.

Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 to 65 mph were reported from 2 miles west through 2 miles east of Hartington.  The winds caused a roof to cave in on a house in Hartington and big trees were uprooted with lots of branches and trees down all over town.  Some irrigation systems were overturned west of Hartington and a trailer there was tipped over and a shed destroyed. East of town some trees were downed and a fence destroyed.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 mph knocked the power out in Orchard and flipped a center pivot 3 miles east of town.
Law enforcement reported thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 mph.
A thunderstorm wind gust estimated at 60 mph was reported in Creighton.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 mph downed large tree branches in town.

A Nebraska Department of Roads sensor 3 miles south of David City measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 78 mph.  The strong winds caused scattered tree, fence and house damage in the David City area and surrounding communities.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 70 mph downed numerous large trees southeast of Brainard.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 70 mph knocked a very large tree onto a garage destroying half of it.  Other tree damage was noted in town.
A local mesonet observation near the Washington county/Douglas county line south of Blair measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph.

Local media weather equipment measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph in the Wahoo area.  The winds knocked down a few tree limbs in town but overall the damage was nothing major according to the county Emergency Manager.
A spotter estimated thunderstorm wind gusts around 60 mph in the Harlan area.
A spotter in the Irwin area stated that healthy tree branches, some up to a few inches in diameter, were downed by thunderstorm winds that were estimated at close to 60 mph.
